raw_case_text:
A 50-year-old gentleman, resident of a slum area in the outskirts of New Delhi, presented to surgery emergency with complaints of diffuse abdominal pain for 5 days, obstipation for 2 days, and abdominal distension for 1 day. There was a history of recurrent episodes of loose stools mixed with mucous and blood associated with intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain for the past 7 days. The patient was a chronic alcoholic and a known case of diabetes mellitus. On examination, the patient was dehydrated, pulse rate was 120/min, and blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, and was maintaining a saturation of 98% on room air. The abdomen was grossly distended and tenderness was present all over. Rectal examination done later revealed distended rectum and examining finger was tinged with blood and foul-smelling mucous.
The patient was resuscitated with intravenous fluids following which he improved to BP 100/72 mm Hg, PR 102/min, RR 17/min, and urine output of 200 ml over 4 hours. After stabilization, the patient was shifted for chest and abdominal X-ray, which showed gas under the diaphragm (Figure 1). ABG analysis showed mild metabolic acidosis which got corrected with fluid resuscitation. Hemoglobin was 8.2 gm%, total leucocyte counts were 24000/mm3, blood urea was 72 mg/dl, and serum creatinine was 1.8 mg/dl. Serum electrolytes and coagulation profile were within the normal range. (Na 136 mEq/L, K 4.2 mEq/L, INR 1.2).
The patient was started on ceftriaxone and metronidazole as per our institutional protocol and amikacin was added after one day when KFTs became normal. The patient was taken up for emergency laparotomy. Approximately 1000 ml of feculent pyoperitoneum was present. The caecum was found to be gangrenous and had sloughed off (Figure 2) and there were multiple perforations in the ascending colon and transverse colon. Initially, right hemicolectomy was done but the resected end of the transverse colon showed multiple sloughed off ulcers in the mucosa with transmural involvement. The proximal sigmoid colon was also found to be perforated into the retroperitoneum. There was no evidence of thrombosis of mesenteric vessels. In view of intraoperative findings, the procedure was converted into subtotal colectomy with proximal ileostomy and exteriorization of the distal end of the sigmoid colon.
Gross examination of the resected colectomy specimen showed sloughed off caecum with multiple perforations in the ascending, transverse, and descending colon (Figure 3). On cut section examination, there were patchy segments of extensive transmural necrosis with multiple defects ranging from 0.5-2 cm throughout the large bowel (Figure 4). Histopathological examination of the specimen showed findings of multiple mucosal ulcerations with liquefactive necrosis with normal intervening mucosa, associated with full-thickness perforations and extensive diffuse transmural inflammation. The ulcers were typically flask-shaped, with a narrow neck and broad, undermined base. In the colon, there was no evidence of architectural distortion or any evidence of crypt destructive colitis or granulomas to support the presence of Crohn's disease. The colonic mucosal ulcers were covered with neutrophilic debris within which E. histolytica were identified (Figure 5). Pathogenic Entamoebae trophozoites were recognized by the presence of phagocytosed ingested intracellular red cells. Periodic acid-Schiff staining was positive (Figure 6). Amoebic serology was positive with high IgM antibody titers (2.24) <0.04.
The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged on day 8 and was continued on oral metronidazole for 2 weeks and the luminal amoebicidal agent, diloxanide furoate, for 10 days. The patient underwent surgery for restoration of continuity of the bowel after 3 months and ileorectal anastomosis was done. The patient was healthy and symptom-free up to 2 months of follow-up in OPD.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male from a New Delhi slum presented to the surgical emergency department with 5 days of diffuse abdominal pain, 2 days of obstipation, and 1 day of abdominal distension preceded by 7 days of bloody, mucoid diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Seven days prior to presentation, the patient developed recurrent loose stools mixed with blood and mucus accompanied by intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain. Over the preceding 5 days, the pain became diffuse and continuous, followed by complete obstipation for 2 days and progressive abdominal distension for 1 day.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known history of diabetes mellitus and chronic alcoholism; resident of an urban slum area on the outskirts of New Delhi.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for bloody mucoid diarrhea (7 days), diffuse abdominal pain (5 days), obstipation (2 days), and abdominal distension (1 day).

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: dehydrated, pulse rate 120/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air (improving after IV fluid resuscitation to BP 100/72 mmHg, PR 102/min, RR 17/min, urine output 200 mL/4h). Abdominal exam: grossly distended with generalized tenderness. Digital rectal exam: distended rectum with examining finger stained with blood and foul-smelling mucus.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory results: hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, leukocytosis (TLC 24,000/mm3), blood urea 72 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (normalizing after 1 day of resuscitation), sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, INR 1.2, and mild metabolic acidosis on arterial blood gas (corrected with fluids). Erect chest and abdominal X-rays demonstrated free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum) under the diaphragm.
objective.advanced_workup: Emergency exploratory laparotomy revealed ~1000 mL of feculent pyoperitoneum, a gangrenous sloughed-off cecum, multiple transmural perforations across the ascending and transverse colon, retroperitoneal perforation of the proximal sigmoid colon, and patent mesenteric vessels; initial right hemicolectomy was converted intraoperatively to a subtotal colectomy with proximal end ileostomy and distal sigmoid exteriorization.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Histopathological examination of the subtotal colectomy specimen demonstrated classic flask-shaped mucosal ulcers with liquefactive transmural necrosis, normal intervening mucosa (no granulomas or crypt distortion to suggest Crohn's disease), and Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites containing ingested erythrocytes within the neutrophilic surface debris, corroborated by positive serum anti-amoebic IgM serology (titer 2.24, reference <0.04), confirming fulminant necrotizing amoebic colitis with multiple colonic perforations and feculent peritonitis. Following subtotal colectomy with ileostomy, IV fluid resuscitation, and inpatient IV ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and amikacin, he was discharged on postoperative day 8 on oral metronidazole (2 weeks) and luminal diloxanide furoate (10 days), underwent successful ileorectal anastomosis at 3 months, and remained asymptomatic at 2-month follow-up.
